backTranslations.41:
**Before the appointment**
- Enter the date of the appointment in the Appointment tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are, and what would make them stronger.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most. Stick to three or four.
- Make the notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**During the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be readable in under a minute: counts, averages, the hot flash calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can make the notes in that language.

**What the notes are, and are not**

They are a summary of what you have recorded, plus what you yourself chose to bring in from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or a complete medical record, and any patterns in them are coincidence checks, not proof of cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add any new medication with a start date. In a few weeks MenoMap can show your entries before and after, which makes the next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day that marks 12 months in a row without a period, when it is not due to something else (such as pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but anything from the mid-40s to the mid-50s is common.

**Perimenopause** is the years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, closer together or further apart. Many of the changes people associate with the change of life, such as hot flashes, night sweats, changes in sleep and changes in mood, often start here, while you still have periods. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably longer, and it looks different for everyone.

**Postmenopause** is everything after the twelve-month mark. Some symptoms calm down over time; others can continue for years.

Menopause can also come earlier because of an operation where the ovaries are removed, certain cancer treatments or other health conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth raising with a doctor.

**How it is recognised.** In many people over 45, the doctor recognises perimenopause or menopause from your medical history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always necessary, because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. They are more often used when someone is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which phase you are in. What MenoMap can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, on the neck and on the chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, palpitations or chills afterwards. Night sweats are the same during sleep, and can be strong enough to wake you or make the bedding soaked.

They are among the most common changes around the change of life. Some have a few mild flashes; others have many a day that disrupt work and sleep. In some they go away within a few years; in others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Many notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, warm rooms, stress or heavy bedding. This varies a lot from person to person, and so it can be more useful to follow your own tags than to use a general list.

**There are other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also come from thyroid problems, infections, certain medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or come together with weight loss, fever or feeling ill, mention it to a doctor.

**Describe them well.** Useful details for an appointment:
- Roughly how many per day and per night
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to come before them
- What you have tried, and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's Wave button and after-the-fact logging exist to capture exactly this without much effort.

**Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, in addition to practical measures. Which ones suit you is something to talk to a doctor about.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces some of the estrogen the body makes less of around the change of life. Major guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gel, spray, tablets and low-dose products for use in the vagina for local symptoms such as dryness. Those who still have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen in addition to estrogen to protect the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, how long since the periods stopped, own medical history and family history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and what type of treatment it is and how it is taken. That is why it is a decision you make together with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app can decide.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- What type and form would you suggest, and why?
- What benefits can I expect, and how quickly?
- What is my personal risk, and how does it compare with not treating?
- What should I watch for, and when should we reconsider it?

**If you already use it,** record it in MenoMap (You → Medications). MenoMap shows your waves before and after you started, as a coincidence check and not as proof, so you have something concrete to talk about at the next review.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not right for everyone, and some simply prefer other paths. There are several.

**Prescription alternatives.** Some non-hormonal medications have documented effect against hot flashes. Among them are some medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer group of drugs made specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them against each other.

**Talking and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted to the change of life has documented effect in making hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improving sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes many find helpful:**
- Clothes in layers that you can quickly take off
- A fan at the desk and by the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and dampening personal triggers (the tags and experiments in MenoMap help with this)
- Regular activity and a fixed sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal preparations.** The evidence is mixed or limited for many of them, quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own records before and during a change, and that is easier to assess than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it is hard to remember a month of nights in the moment. One tends to remember the last days or the worst ones. A simple record fills the gap.

**This is what a diary gives your doctor:**
- How often symptoms come and how strong they are, not just that they come
- Whether things are getting better, worse or staying the same
- What happened around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point to compare with if you try a treatment

**Keep it simple.** A diary only helps if you keep it. MenoMap is built around a one-tap Wave button and an evening check-in with four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of entries usually gives a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. The Appointment tab in MenoMap helps you choose questions and prints them together with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
When 12 months have passed without a period, **all bleeding from the vagina should be examined by a doctor**, even if it only happened once, and even if it was only spotting or light pink or brown discharge.

Most often the cause turns out not to be serious. A thinner lining of the vagina or the uterus, for example, is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when found early. That is why public health advice says you should have it examined instead of waiting.

**If you use hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns can be expected, depending on which type you use. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual or comes at the wrong time should also be examined.

**What you should do:**
- Contact your doctor or the health service and say that you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, how much, and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can keep this for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. The app reminds you to have it examined and includes it in the notes for the appointment.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints in midlife, and it rarely has only one cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or make you too hot or damp to settle again.

**Other common factors:**
- Having to pee at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but often makes sleep more fragmented in the second half of the night
- Caffeine later in the day
- Pain, restless legs or a partner who snores
- Snoring or breathing pauses, which can be signs of sleep apnoea (worth raising, especially if you are very sleepy in the daytime)

**This often helps.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layered clothes you can take off; a fixed time to get up; and less alcohol near bedtime. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied method, and many doctors can point you to it.

**This is what you can track.** For a week or two you can note sleep score, waves at night, alcohol and caffeine late in the day. The evening check-in and the wave log in MenoMap do this with a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside the night sweats, as background and not as explanation.

**When you should get it checked.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example when you drive), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice breathing pauses or gasping for air at night.
